prompt: Which Azure service is a REGIONAL layer-7 (HTTP/S) load balancer?
choices: Azure Application Gateway
Azure Traffic Manager profiles
Azure Front Door Premium
Azure Firewall Premium
explanation: Application Gateway is the regional layer-7 load balancer; Front Door is its global counterpart, and Traffic Manager is DNS-based global routing (not layer-7).

prompt: Which Azure service is a GLOBAL layer-7 entry point that includes CDN, acceleration, and failover?
choices: Azure Front Door
Azure Application Gateway
Azure Firewall Premium
Azure Bastion hosts
explanation: Front Door is the global layer-7 edge with CDN caching and failover, whereas Application Gateway is regional. Scope is the whole distinction, and it is what decides the design: a multi-region app fronted by a regional gateway sends every user through one region.

prompt: How is a Web Application Firewall (WAF) deployed in Azure?
choices: As a policy on Application Gateway or Front Door
As a standalone appliance in its own dedicated subnet
As a module running inside Azure Bastion
As a built-in feature of every NSG
correctAnswers: As a policy on Application Gateway or Front Door
explanation: A WAF is a policy attached to Application Gateway or Front Door, never a standalone appliance. Expecting a dedicated subnet is the on-premises instinct, whereas in Azure the WAF has no existence of its own — it configures an existing layer-7 entry point.

prompt: At which layers does Azure Firewall operate and what does it filter?
choices: Layers 3 to 7, general VNet traffic
Layer 7 only, filtering web-application attacks
Layer 2 only, filtering by MAC address
Layer 4 only, filtering by port number
explanation: Azure Firewall is a general-purpose stateful firewall spanning layers 3 to 7, with both network and application rules. Reading it as layer 7 only is the confusion with a WAF: Azure Firewall does inspect FQDNs, whereas it does not parse HTTP bodies for injection.

prompt: Which best distinguishes Azure Firewall from a Web Application Firewall?
choices: Firewall filters network traffic; a WAF blocks web attacks
A WAF filters all VNet traffic; Azure Firewall only inspects HTTP
Azure Firewall is layer 3 only; a WAF operates at layer 4
They are the same product under different SKUs
correctAnswers: Firewall filters network traffic; a WAF blocks web attacks
explanation: Azure Firewall filters general network traffic; a WAF blocks web-application attacks in HTTP. This is the most frequently tested distinction in the domain, and neither substitutes for the other — a WAF cannot control egress by FQDN, whereas a firewall cannot see SQL injection in a request body.

prompt: What does Azure Firewall Manager provide?
choices: Central management of many firewalls and reusable policies
A single firewall instance, with no policy reuse across VNets
A dashboard for the Secure Score recommendations
Vulnerability scanning of the firewall rules
correctAnswers: Central management of many firewalls and reusable policies
explanation: Firewall Manager centralises multiple firewalls and reusable firewall policies at scale. It is not a single firewall instance, which is the misreading — the value is precisely that one policy object applies to many firewalls rather than being copied into each.

prompt: Which WAF mode actively blocks malicious requests rather than only logging them?
choices: Prevention mode
Detection-only mode
Monitor mode
Passive mode
explanation: Prevention mode blocks matching requests, whereas Detection mode only logs them. The two look identical in the portal until traffic arrives, which is why deploying straight into Prevention without a Detection pilot is how a WAF takes down a working application.

prompt: Which managed rule set provides baseline WAF protection against common web attacks?
choices: OWASP Core Rule Set
MITRE ATT&CK rule set
CIS Benchmark rule set
PCI-DSS rule set
explanation: The OWASP Core Rule Set is the standard managed rule set Azure WAF uses. MITRE ATT&CK and CIS are tempting because they are equally well-known security frameworks, however neither is a WAF rule set — they describe adversary behaviour and configuration baselines rather than HTTP signatures.

prompt: Which two DDoS Protection tiers exist as of 2026, and how do they differ?
choices: Network Protection and IP Protection
DDoS Basic and Premium, differing in speed
DDoS Protection is only a WAF feature
Only DDoS Protection Standard exists
explanation: Both tiers share the same mitigation engine: Network Protection adds rapid-response support, cost protection and WAF discount, whereas IP Protection is billed per protected IP. Believing they differ in mitigation speed is the misconception, since the detection and mitigation are identical.

prompt: Older material references 'DDoS Protection Standard'. Which current portal tier does this correspond to?
choices: DDoS Network Protection
Azure Firewall Premium tier
DDoS IP Protection tier
The DDoS Basic tier
explanation: DDoS Protection Standard is the previous branding of what is now DDoS Network Protection. IP Protection is the closest miss and a genuinely different tier rather than a rename, which is why matching old material to new names matters here.

prompt: Where do you enforce a minimum TLS version for an App Service or API Management instance?
choices: In the service's TLS/SSL settings
In an Azure Firewall application rule
In a UDR next-hop configuration
In the subnet NSG rule set
explanation: The minimum TLS version is set on the service itself, in its TLS/SSL settings. An Azure Firewall application rule is the tempting answer because it also concerns traffic to the app, however it filters by FQDN rather than negotiating the connection.

prompt: A public API needs global reach, low latency across continents, a CDN, and protection against OWASP attacks. Which fits best?
choices: Azure Front Door with a WAF policy
Azure Application Gateway alone
Azure Firewall with application rules
A private endpoint plus a service endpoint
correctAnswers: Azure Front Door with a WAF policy
explanation: Global reach with low latency and a CDN points to Front Door, and attaching a WAF policy adds the OWASP protection. Application Gateway alone is the closest miss and fails on scope: it is regional, so users on other continents still traverse one region.

prompt: A regional web app needs a layer-7 load balancer with path-based routing and a WAF, but no global CDN. Which service fits best?
choices: Application Gateway with a WAF policy
Azure Traffic Manager with a WAF policy
Azure Front Door with a WAF policy
Azure Firewall Premium instead
correctAnswers: Application Gateway with a WAF policy
explanation: A regional app needing path-based routing is Application Gateway with a WAF policy. Front Door is the tempting upgrade, but paying for a global edge and CDN when there is no global audience buys latency and cost rather than protection.

prompt: Which statement about where a WAF can be attached is correct?
choices: It attaches to Application Gateway or Front Door
A WAF policy can only be attached to Azure Firewall Premium
A WAF policy attaches to a VPN Gateway
A WAF policy attaches to an NSG rule set
correctAnswers: It attaches to Application Gateway or Front Door
explanation: A WAF policy attaches to Application Gateway or Front Door, and to nothing else. It never attaches to an NSG or a VPN gateway, which is the confusion these lists invite — those operate at layers 3 and 4 and cannot parse HTTP at all.

prompt: Which capability is specific to Azure Firewall (and not to a WAF)?
choices: FQDN and threat-intelligence egress filtering
Blocking SQL injection in an HTTP request body
Terminating TLS for a web listener
Enforcing the OWASP Core Rule Set
explanation: FQDN filtering and threat-intelligence filtering of general network traffic are Azure Firewall capabilities. The three distractors are all WAF functions, and that split is the point: a firewall decides where traffic may go, whereas a WAF decides what an HTTP request may contain.

prompt: You want a WAF that logs suspicious requests without blocking legitimate users during an initial tuning period. Which mode should you start in?
choices: Detection mode
Prevention mode
Disabled mode
Bypass mode
explanation: Detection mode logs matches without blocking, which is what makes it the tuning mode before switching to Prevention. Going straight to Prevention is the tempting shortcut, however untuned OWASP rules produce false positives that block real users.

prompt: Which service would you recommend to protect a set of critical public IPs against volumetric attacks with rapid-response support and cost protection?
choices: Azure DDoS Network Protection
A Web Application Firewall in Prevention
Azure DDoS IP Protection tier
Azure Firewall Premium tier
explanation: Rapid-response support and cost protection are exclusive to DDoS Network Protection, which is what a set of critical public IPs warrants. IP Protection is the closest miss: same mitigation engine, whereas the value-added services are absent.

prompt: A cost-sensitive team wants baseline volumetric DDoS mitigation on just a handful of public IPs, without paying for rapid-response support. Which tier fits?
choices: DDoS IP Protection
DDoS Basic, once purchased
DDoS Network Protection
Azure Front Door Premium
explanation: DDoS IP Protection is billed per protected IP with the same mitigation engine, minus the value-added services — exactly the cost-sensitive choice. DDoS Basic is the tempting answer and does not need buying at all, since it is the free always-on platform protection rather than a tier.

prompt: An internal-only API must be published to the internet but protected against OWASP attacks and highly available in one region. Which pairing is most appropriate?
choices: Application Gateway WAF v2 fronting the API
A private endpoint on the API with public access enabled
A service endpoint plus an NSG allow rule
Azure Firewall with a DNAT rule only
correctAnswers: Application Gateway WAF v2 fronting the API
explanation: Fronting the API with an Application Gateway WAF v2, and keeping the API itself off the public internet, publishes it with OWASP protection in path. An Azure Firewall DNAT rule is the tempting alternative and it publishes the API without inspecting the HTTP at all.

prompt: Which is TRUE about Front Door versus Application Gateway regarding scope?
choices: Front Door is global; Gateway is regional
Application Gateway is global; Front Door is regional
Both of them are strictly regional
Both of them are strictly global in scope
correctAnswers: Front Door is global; Gateway is regional
explanation: Front Door is global and Application Gateway is regional — that scope difference is the defining one. Both can host a WAF, which is why answering on WAF capability rather than on scope misses what distinguishes them.

prompt: What is the main security purpose of enforcing a minimum TLS version on an app?
choices: To reject clients negotiating weak versions
To encrypt the data at rest in the app's storage
To block the OWASP injection attacks
To provide volumetric DDoS mitigation
correctAnswers: To reject clients negotiating weak versions
explanation: A minimum TLS version rejects clients that would negotiate weak, deprecated protocol versions, closing a downgrade path. It is unrelated to at-rest encryption or to OWASP attacks, which is the conflation to avoid: transport strength cannot stop an injection payload carried over a perfectly modern TLS session.

prompt: Which component would you use to centrally apply the SAME set of firewall rules to several Azure Firewalls deployed in different regions?
choices: A policy managed in Azure Firewall Manager
A separate rule collection copied into each firewall
An NSG applied to each firewall's own subnet
A UDR shared across all of the regions
correctAnswers: A policy managed in Azure Firewall Manager
explanation: A firewall policy managed in Firewall Manager is a reusable object applied across many firewalls, so one edit propagates. Copying a rule collection into each firewall is the tempting manual equivalent, however the copies drift the moment one is edited locally.

prompt: A WAF in Prevention mode is blocking a legitimate application request that resembles an attack pattern. What is the appropriate remediation?
choices: Add a targeted rule exclusion or custom rule
Switch the whole WAF policy to Detection mode permanently
Delete the OWASP Core Rule Set from it
Disable the WAF policy on the gateway
correctAnswers: Add a targeted rule exclusion or custom rule
explanation: False positives are handled with narrow exclusions or custom rules, preserving protection elsewhere — not by disabling the WAF or dropping the rule set.

prompt: Which layer-7 service natively provides content caching at edge locations near users?
choices: Azure Front Door (CDN)
Azure Application Gateway
Azure VPN Gateway v2
Azure Firewall Premium
explanation: Front Door includes CDN edge caching and acceleration, whereas Application Gateway is a regional load balancer with no caching at all. That absence is what makes Application Gateway the wrong answer to a latency requirement stated in terms of geography.

prompt: Which two statements correctly distinguish Application Gateway from Front Door? (Choose two.)
choices: Application Gateway is regional
Front Door is global, with CDN
Application Gateway provides global edge caching
Neither of them can host a WAF policy
correctAnswers: Front Door is global, with CDN
explanation: Application Gateway is regional and Front Door is global with CDN. Neither distractor holds: both services can host a WAF policy, whereas only Front Door provides global edge caching.

prompt: Which two statements about Azure DDoS IP Protection are correct? (Choose two.)
choices: It is priced per protected IP address
It shares the mitigation engine with Network Protection
It includes rapid response support, and cost protection too
It is a feature of the Web Application Firewall
correctAnswers: It is priced per protected IP address
It shares the mitigation engine with Network Protection
explanation: IP Protection is per-IP and shares the engine, but omits rapid response and cost protection, which are Network Protection value-adds.

prompt: Which two are capabilities of a Web Application Firewall? (Choose two.)
choices: Blocking SQL injection and cross-site scripting
Applying the OWASP Core Rule Set
Filtering general egress traffic by FQDN as well
Providing volumetric DDoS cost protection too
correctAnswers: Blocking SQL injection and cross-site scripting
Applying the OWASP Core Rule Set
explanation: Blocking SQL injection and cross-site scripting, and applying the OWASP Core Rule Set, are WAF capabilities. FQDN egress filtering belongs to Azure Firewall and DDoS cost protection to the Network Protection tier — both tempting because they are neighbouring network controls.

prompt: Referring to requirement 5 (internal API reachable from the internet, protected against SQLi/XSS, global low-latency reach), which solution fits best?
choices: Front Door with a WAF in Prevention mode
Azure Application Gateway without any WAF policy
Azure Firewall with application rules only
A private endpoint on the API instead
correctAnswers: Front Door with a WAF in Prevention mode
explanation: Global reach points to Front Door, and OWASP protection requires an attached WAF policy in Prevention mode. Application Gateway without a WAF is the closest miss and fails on both counts: regional scope, and no rule set inspecting the requests.

prompt: Referring to requirement 6 (protect critical public IPs from volumetric DDoS with full mitigation support, rapid response, and cost protection), which tier should Fabrikam choose?
choices: DDoS Network Protection tier
The default protection on every public IP
DDoS IP Protection instead
A WAF policy in Prevention
explanation: Rapid response and cost protection are exclusive to the Network Protection tier; IP Protection shares the engine but omits them.

prompt: Fabrikam's WAF (Prevention mode) in front of the internal API is blocking one legitimate request shape used by a partner integration. What is the correct action?
choices: Add a scoped exclusion for that request shape
Move the API behind Application Gateway instead of Front Door
Switch the WAF to Detection mode for all traffic
Remove the OWASP Core Rule Set from the policy
correctAnswers: Add a scoped exclusion for that request shape
explanation: A scoped exclusion or custom rule resolves the false positive while the rest of the OWASP protection stays active. Switching the whole policy to Detection is the tempting quick fix, but it disables blocking for every request rather than for the one request shape that misfires.

prompt: Order the steps to safely put a WAF into active blocking in front of a regional web app.
reorderItems: Create an Application Gateway (WAF v2 SKU) fronting the app
Create a WAF policy with the OWASP Core Rule Set
Set the WAF policy mode to Detection and review the logs
Switch the WAF policy mode to Prevention
explanation: The gateway and its WAF policy must exist before any tuning, whereas piloting in Detection before switching to Prevention is what prevents a self-inflicted outage. Going straight to Prevention is the ordering mistake that blocks legitimate traffic on day one.

prompt: Order the steps to protect a set of critical public IPs with DDoS Network Protection.
reorderItems: Associate the protection plan with the virtual network containing the public IPs
Enable DDoS Network Protection on that virtual network
Review DDoS telemetry and configure alerting
explanation: The DDoS plan must exist and be linked to the virtual network before protection is active, whereas monitoring is configured afterwards. Expecting the plan alone to protect anything is the omission: an unlinked plan bills without defending.

prompt: Configure this simplified WAF policy screen for a global public API needing OWASP protection, attached to Front Door.
explanation: Prevention actively blocks, the OWASP Core Rule Set provides baseline coverage, and a WAF attaches to Front Door (or Application Gateway) — not Azure Firewall.

prompt: Proposed solution: Front Door with a WAF policy in Prevention mode using the OWASP Core Rule Set. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
explanation: Front Door delivers global low-latency reach, whereas the attached WAF in Prevention mode blocks OWASP-class attacks — the two halves of the goal need both components. Note the operational cost it accepts: Prevention mode needs tuning first, or legitimate requests are blocked.

prompt: Proposed solution: Azure Firewall with application rules only, no Front Door. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
explanation: Azure Firewall filters general network traffic; it provides neither OWASP web-attack protection nor global CDN-backed low-latency reach.

prompt: Proposed solution: Application Gateway alone, in a single region, without Front Door or a WAF. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
explanation: Without a WAF there's no OWASP protection, and a single regional Application Gateway does not provide global low-latency reach.

prompt: Complete the command that enforces a minimum TLS version of 1.2 on an App Service.
template: az webapp config set --name App1 --resource-group RG1 [[b1]] [[b2]]
explanation: App Service expresses the floor as `1.2`, whereas a storage account expresses the same setting as `TLS1_2` — the inconsistency between services is exactly what gets copied wrongly from one script to another. `--https-only` is the tempting neighbour and answers a different question: it forces the connection to be encrypted at all, rather than rejecting the weak protocol versions a client might negotiate.

prompt: Build the sequence that puts VNet1's public IPs under DDoS Network Protection. Not every action in the pool belongs in the answer.
poolItems: Create a DDoS protection plan in the subscription
Link the plan to VNet1 and enable DDoS protection on the virtual network
Configure DDoS metric alerts so an attack raises a notification
Attach the plan directly to each public IP address
Downgrade the public IP SKU to Basic to reduce the attack surface
Add a WAF policy in Prevention mode to the DDoS plan
correctOrder: Create a DDoS protection plan in the subscription
Link the plan to VNet1 and enable DDoS protection on the virtual network
Configure DDoS metric alerts so an attack raises a notification
explanation: A plan that is not linked to a virtual network bills without defending anything, which is the omission this item exists to catch. Protection is enabled on the VNet, so it covers the Standard public IPs of resources in it — never on a subnet, and never on an individual IP under Network Protection. Basic-SKU public IPs cannot be protected at all, so downgrading removes the protection instead of tightening it, and a WAF policy attaches to Application Gateway or Front Door rather than to a DDoS plan.

prompt: Complete the command that switches an Application Gateway WAF policy from logging matches to actively blocking them.
template: az network application-gateway waf-policy policy-setting update --policy-name WafPol1 --resource-group RG1 --mode [[b1]] --state [[b2]]
explanation: The two modes are Detection and Prevention: Detection logs a match and lets the request through, Prevention blocks it. Blocking and Enforce are the words people expect and neither exists, so the command fails rather than half-working. The state must also be Enabled — a policy in Prevention mode but disabled inspects nothing, which is the configuration that looks correct in a review and protects nothing in production.

prompt: Which command creates the reusable Azure Firewall policy object that Firewall Manager applies across several firewalls?
choices: az network firewall policy create
az network application-gateway waf-policy create
az network firewall network-rule create
az network firewall ip-config create
explanation: A firewall policy is a standalone object that many firewalls can reference, which is what makes one edit propagate instead of being copied into each. The WAF policy command is the closest miss by name and creates something for a different service: Application Gateway or Front Door, inspecting HTTP rather than filtering network traffic. The other two work inside a firewall — its rules and its IP configuration — instead of producing the shareable policy.

prompt: One web app must refuse protocol versions below 1.2 while the other apps sharing its App Service plan keep their current setting. Complete the Azure PowerShell command.
explanation: The TLS floor is a property of the app, so it is set on the web app. `Set-AzAppServicePlan` is the tempting neighbour and cannot carry it: a plan is the compute container, and several apps on one plan can each have a different minimum. `-SslState` belongs to a custom-domain binding and governs whether a hostname requires SNI or IP-based SSL, rather than which protocol versions are refused.

prompt: Volumetric DDoS protection with cost protection and rapid-response support is required for three public IP addresses on one virtual network. No other public IPs exist. The solution must minimize cost.
choices: Azure DDoS IP Protection
Azure DDoS Network Protection
A WAF policy in Prevention mode
Azure Firewall Premium on the hub
explanation: IP Protection bills per protected address and shares the mitigation engine with the network tier, so three addresses cost far less than a plan. Network Protection is the trap: it delivers the same mitigation and the same support, but it is priced per plan covering up to 100 addresses, which three cannot justify. A WAF answers application-layer attacks rather than volumetric ones.

prompt: A web application is served from three Azure regions and must be protected against the OWASP top ten. Requests must be inspected as close to the client as possible, and the solution must leave no gaps in coverage across the three regions. What should you deploy?
choices: Front Door with a WAF policy
An Application Gateway per region
Azure Firewall Premium per region
A WAF policy attached to each NSG
correctAnswers: Front Door with a WAF policy
explanation: Front Door inspects at the global edge, so a single WAF policy covers all three regions with nothing to keep in step. Three regional Application Gateways would also protect every region and is the tempting answer, but inspection then happens after the request has reached a region, and three policies can drift apart — the coverage requirement is what rules it out, not its capability. A WAF policy cannot attach to an NSG at all.

prompt: Twelve Azure Firewall instances across four regions must share one rule set, and regional operators must be able to read the rules but never edit them. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege for those operators.
choices: A Firewall Manager policy
A rule collection in each firewall
An ARM template per firewall
A shared UDR across the regions
explanation: A Firewall Manager policy is a resource of its own, so read access on it can be granted separately from the firewalls the operators run. Copying a rule collection into each firewall reaches the same filtering and is the obvious approach, but editing rules then requires write access on the firewall itself, so the operators inevitably get more than reading. ARM templates deploy configuration without governing who may change it afterwards.
